title: Annual recurring revenue (ARR)
reading_md:
**Setting.** The examples use Business Care, the device-support subscription Voltmarkt sells to small offices. It is billed monthly; Business Care Year is the same support paid for a year in advance.

**What it measures.** The yearly run rate of recurring revenue: what a year of subscription revenue would come to if this month's MRR stayed the same for 12 months.

**Formula.**

ARR = MRR × 12

- Use the MRR of a complete month, with every active plan at its full monthly amount.
- Business Care Year is in MRR at a twelfth of its yearly fee in every month it covers, so in ARR it counts once, at its yearly fee.
- One-off fees stay out, as they do in MRR.
- Grain: month.

**Worked example.** In September 2026 Business Care had 420 businesses at €40 a month and 60 on Business Care Year at €420 a year.

- MRR = 420 × 40 + 60 × 420 / 12 = 16,800 + 2,100 = €18,900.
- ARR = 18,900 × 12 = €226,800.

On 15 October a dashboard shows October's MRR so far as €9,500, because only the businesses billed so far are in it. 9,500 × 12 = €114,000 is not a run rate. A month still in progress understates ARR: use September until October is complete.

**What ARR is not.**

- Revenue earned over the last 12 months. When MRR grows during the year, ARR is above last year's revenue.
- Cash collected. A Business Care Year business pays for the whole year at once, but adds the same amount to ARR in every month its plan covers.
- A forecast. It assumes nothing changes: no new businesses, no cancellations.

**Common mistakes.**

- Multiplying the MRR of a month that is not complete.
- Counting a yearly plan's whole fee in MRR and then multiplying by 12.
- Adding one-off fees.

**What it does not answer.**

- Whether existing customers stay and grow: that is NRR and GRR.
- How many customers left: that is logo churn.

**How managers ask for it.** "What's our ARR run rate?" "Are we at €300,000 ARR yet?"
